messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 39
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: City Council Member
- Trauma Type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
- Pcl5: 54

She is 39, a European woman who serves on the city council, and at first glance her life looks composed, articulate, and public-facing. She is practiced at speaking in measured tones, at holding eye contact, at appearing steady while other people become emotional. Over several conversations, though, the steadiness begins to feel less like ease and more like something she has built carefully over many years.

She grows up in a small apartment where evenings are unpredictable. Her father’s moods govern the atmosphere of the home. Some nights there is laughter at dinner, the television on, plates cleared without incident. Other nights she can tell from the way the front door opens that everything in her body needs to prepare. As a child, she becomes exquisitely alert to sound: the scrape of a chair, the heaviness of footsteps in the hallway, the sudden sharpness in her father’s voice, the soft, placating tone her mother uses when trying to calm him. She never describes being the one directly hit. What she remembers most vividly is watching. She stands in the doorway of her bedroom, or crouches halfway down the hall, listening to her parents in the kitchen. She sees her father slam his fist into the wall beside her mother’s head, sees him grab her arm hard enough to leave marks, sees a glass shatter on the floor. Her mother tells her afterward to go back to bed, that everything is fine now. It is never fine, and it is never over.

She learns early that fear has to be hidden. In school she is quiet, high-achieving, unusually mature. Teachers praise her self-discipline. At home she tries to make herself useful—washing dishes quickly, helping her younger sibling with homework, staying out of the way. At night she lies awake listening for movement. Even when the apartment is silent, her body remains braced, as if something terrible is still approaching. She begins to have vivid images that arrive uninvited during the day: her mother pinned against the counter, her father’s face changed by rage, the sound of breaking glass. Sometimes a raised male voice at school makes her heart pound so suddenly that she cannot follow what the teacher is saying. She feels ashamed by how frightened she is and tells no one.

As a teenager, she spends more time away from home and becomes fiercely organized. She tells herself that she will build a life governed by rules, civility, and accountability. Politics begins to make sense to her before she has language for why. Public order, process, committee meetings, policy debates—these feel safer than private chaos. In university and then in local government work, she is known as diligent, calm under pressure, and relentlessly prepared. She marries a kind man who is patient and emotionally available, and she experiences him at times as a refuge, at times as someone whose nearness makes her unexpectedly tense. When they argue, even mildly, she feels a rush of panic that seems out of proportion to the moment. If his voice sharpens in frustration, she stops hearing the content of what he is saying. Her chest tightens, her thoughts go blank, and she scans for exits without meaning to. Later she feels embarrassed and angry with herself, insisting that she is not a child anymore.

In her work as a city council member, she is respected for her command of contentious meetings. Yet conflict affects her more than others can see. During heated council sessions, especially when men interrupt one another or pound the table for emphasis, she feels a familiar surge in her body—adrenaline, heat, a trembling she hides by gripping her pen under the desk. She is acutely sensitive to shifts in tone and can predict escalation before anyone else in the room seems to notice. Colleagues admire this political instinct. She experiences it less as intuition than as an old survival skill that never turned off.

She avoids certain stories in her constituency work. When cases involve domestic disputes, she delegates if she can, telling herself it is about workload. If she cannot avoid them, she becomes consumed afterward. She checks locks repeatedly before bed. Sleep is shallow and easily broken. She wakes from dreams in which she is back in the hallway of her childhood home, unable to move, unable to call out to her mother. On those nights she walks through the house to make sure everything is secure, though she knows rationally that her father has been dead for years and that her husband is asleep in the next room.

She speaks about her mother with a complicated tenderness. Part of her understands how trapped her mother was; another part still carries the child’s fury that no one protected them. She rarely visits the neighborhood where she grew up. When a campaign event once brings her near her old street, she notices her hands shaking on the steering wheel and realizes she has been holding her breath.

What troubles her most now is not only the memories themselves, but how present they remain. She has spent decades becoming accomplished, articulate, and publicly effective, yet inside she still feels governed by anticipation. She moves through civic life as someone committed to safety, fairness, and control, while privately enduring sudden images, startle, dread, and a chronic readiness for harm. She says she is tired of living as if the next slammed door might change everything.
